What Is a Personal Injury Claim?
A
personal injury

claim is the legal process allowing someone harmed by another party’s negligence to seek financial compensation. In Greeley, these claims typically involve negotiating with the at-fault party’s insurance company to recover damages such as medical expenses, lost wages, and pain and suffering.
Four elements must be established to bring a valid claim:
the at-fault party

owed you a duty of care, they breached that duty, the breach caused your injury, and you suffered measurable harm. Colorado follows a modified comparative negligence rule, meaning partial fault does not automatically disqualify you from recovering compensation. As long as your share of fault is below 50 percent, you can still pursue a claim. Any percentage of fault assigned to you will reduce your total recovery proportionally, but it does not bar you from recovering altogether.
The circumstances behind every injury are different, and the type of claim you file depends on how the accident happened and who was responsible.
Different Types of Greeley Personal Injury Claims We Handle
Dormer Harpring

represents injured people across a wide range of accident types in Greeley and throughout Weld County. Every injury case is different. The evidence needed to prove a truck accident is not the same as the evidence needed for a slip and fall claim. Different cases require different strategies. What it takes to build a motor vehicle case looks different from what it takes to hold a property owner or product manufacturer accountable.
The claims we handle most often include:
Motor Vehicle Accidents
Car, truck, motorcycle, and rideshare crashes on US-34, US-85, and throughout the Greeley metro area.
Truck and Commercial Vehicle Accidents
Crashes involving semi-trucks, delivery vehicles, and other commercial carriers, where federal FMCSA regulations and carrier liability come into play.
Premises Liability
Slip and fall injuries, inadequate security incidents, and other hazards caused by a property owner’s failure to maintain safe conditions.
Dog Bites
Colorado’s strict liability statute holds dog owners responsible for bite injuries regardless of whether the animal had a prior bite history.
Product Liability
Injuries caused by defective products, from auto parts to consumer goods, where the manufacturer or distributor bears responsibility for the harm caused.
Wrongful Death
When a family loses a loved one due to another party’s negligence, we pursue compensation for funeral costs, lost income, and the full impact of the loss on the people left behind.
Pedestrian and Bicycle Accidents
Collisions involving pedestrians and cyclists in which driver negligence is the primary cause.

If your situation does not appear on this list, we encourage you to contact us. Many cases involve overlapping areas of liability, and we evaluate each claim individually to identify all legal options available.
Common Injuries in Personal Injury Cases

Not every injury looks severe at first. Some of the most serious conditions, including traumatic brain injuries and spinal damage, develop or worsen in the days following an accident. Seeking medical attention early is the only way to know what you are actually dealing with.
Injuries we commonly see in personal injury cases include:
Traumatic brain injuries, including concussions and more severe brain trauma
Spinal cord injuries, ranging from herniated discs to partial or complete paralysis
Broken bones, including fractures to the arms, legs, ribs, and pelvis
Soft tissue injuries such as whiplash, sprains, and muscle tears
Burns from vehicle fires, workplace accidents, or motorcycle road rash
Internal injuries, including organ damage and internal bleeding
Scarring and disfigurement carrying both medical and non-economic damages value
Serious injuries usually lead to larger claims. Medical records help show how badly you were hurt. They also help prove the treatment you needed and the costs you faced.
What Compensation Can You Recover in a Personal Injury Claim?

The type of accident matters, but so does understanding the full range of compensation available to you. Colorado law allows injured people to pursue both economic and non-economic damages. As outlined in
Colorado Jury Instructions
, these categories address both the measurable financial impact of an injury and the personal toll it takes on daily life.
Economic Damages

Economic damages cover losses with a clear dollar value. These include medical bills, surgery costs, physical therapy, prescription medication, lost wages, and reduced earning capacity when injuries affect your ability to work long-term. Future medical expenses carry particular weight in serious injury cases, where treatment extends well beyond the initial recovery period and must be carefully calculated to reflect the full cost of care.
Non-Economic Damages

Non-economic damages cover losses that do not come with a receipt or invoice but are just as real. Pain and suffering, emotional distress, loss of enjoyment of life, and permanent disfigurement or disability all fall into this category. Colorado law limits the total amount a court can award for these losses, meaning there is a maximum dollar amount a jury can grant, regardless of the severity of the harm. Under
, legislation passed in 2024, lawmakers increased that limit to better reflect the true impact serious injuries have on a person’s life.
Statute of Limitations in Colorado Injury Claims

Knowing what you can recover matters very little if you miss the deadline to pursue it. Colorado law sets firm deadlines for filing personal injury claims, and missing them typically means losing the right to compensation entirely.
The deadline depends on the type of case. Motor vehicle accident claims, including car, truck, and motorcycle accidents, must be filed within three years under
. Most other personal injury cases, such as slip and fall, premises liability, dog bites, and product liability claims, carry a two-year deadline under
. Wrongful death claims carry a separate two-year window from the date of death under

Some situations can affect those deadlines. Claims against government entities require a formal notice of claim within 182 days of the incident, which is a separate and much shorter deadline than the standard filing window. The three-year period may also be paused in limited situations, such as when the injured person is a minor, when the defendant concealed the cause of the injury, or when the injury was not reasonably discoverable until a later date. These exceptions are narrow and should never be assumed without legal guidance.

Waiting can hurt your case. Evidence disappears, witnesses forget details, and insurance companies gain an advantage when too much time passes. The earlier legal representation begins, the stronger the claim tends to be.
How Do I Know If I Have a Personal Injury Case?

The honest answer is that most people cannot tell on their own, and they should not have to. What matters is recognizing the practical signals that suggest your situation is worth discussing with an attorney.

Some of the clearest indicators are seeking medical treatment after the incident, having the accident documented by law enforcement or witnesses, suffering injuries that affected your ability to work or carry out daily activities, or being hurt by someone whose conduct was clearly careless or reckless. You do not need every one of those to be present. Even one or two can be enough to support a viable claim.

What to Do After an Injury in Greeley

The steps you take in the hours and days after an accident have a direct impact on the strength of any claim that follows. Evidence disappears quickly, memories fade, and insurance companies begin building their version of events almost immediately. Moving with purpose early protects both your health and your legal options.
Here is what to prioritize:
Get Medical Attention Immediately:
Even if injuries seem minor, see a doctor as soon as possible. Some injuries do not show their full severity at the scene, and an early medical record ties your injuries directly to the accident.
Report the Accident:

Call law enforcement for vehicle incidents and notify the property owner or manager if it happened on someone else’s premises. An official report creates an objective record that carries weight with insurers.
Document Everything:
Photograph the scene, your injuries, and any hazardous conditions. Collect names and contact information from any witnesses before they leave.
Do Not Give Recorded Statements:
Adjusters for the at-fault party are not on your side. Decline any recorded statement until you have spoken with an attorney.
Consult a Greeley Personal Injury Lawyer Early:
The sooner legal representation begins, the better positioned your case will be from the start.
The sooner you act, the more options remain available. If you were injured in Greeley or anywhere in Weld County,
Dormer Harpring
